author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Trouble with Requests
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The request came from a man who thought knowing the words gave him the right to hear the song.

Greg was tuning his guitar at Starwake Pier when the stranger approached the stage. He wore a neat jacket and carried a folded program from the last fundraiser.

"Hey, Greg Universe!" he called. "My partner loves that old song you wrote about Rose. Could you play it tonight?"

Greg's fingers stopped moving.

I noticed immediately. His hands had been busy a second earlier, the familiar rhythm of checking strings and adjusting pegs. Now the guitar rested against his knee, and he was staring at the man's program.

"Not tonight," Greg said.

The man laughed.

"Oh, come on. It's a classic. Everybody knows it."

"Yeah. Still not tonight."

The man looked at me.

"Can you talk him into it?"

I felt a hot, unpleasant pressure behind my ribs.

"He's already answered," I said.

The man frowned.

"I was only asking."

"And he's allowed to say no."

"Fans have requests. That's how concerts work."

Greg lowered his eyes.

I wanted to tell the stranger exactly what I thought of a person who made grief into a customer service issue. Instead, I stepped closer to Greg.

"We have to finish setting up," I said. "Please give us room."

The man hesitated, then walked away muttering something about performers being difficult.

For a while Greg said nothing.

He resumed tuning, but the notes came out uneven.

I sat beside him on the low stage.

"Do you want to talk?" I asked.

"Not really."

"Okay."

He looked at me.

"You're not going to tell me he was wrong?"

"You know what he said."

"Yeah."

"I don't need to explain your feelings to you."

Greg stared at the water.

A small breeze moved across the pier. The repaired railings cast long shadows along the boards. Near the shore, Pip was helping Neri hang a notice about the upcoming lantern walk, a community tradition in which people carried lights from one district to another without being asked to declare what they were remembering.

It had begun as a practical way to mark the safest routes after storms. Over time people had made it into a quiet ritual. Some lanterns were for absent family. Some were for a place someone had left. Some were simply for having made it through a difficult season.

No one had to explain theirs.

Greg watched the lights being tested.

"Rose loved the way a song could make a room feel bigger," he said at last.

I turned toward him.

"Is that why you don't want to play it?"

He shook his head.

"That's part of why I do. Sometimes. But not for a stranger who wants to use the memory like a jukebox."

I nodded.

He rubbed his hands together.

"Sometimes I worry that if I stop singing the old songs, it means I'm trying to forget her."

"Do you believe that?"

"No." He looked down. "Maybe on bad days."

I let the silence stay.

Greg had given so much of himself to people who only knew the cheerful version of him. They heard a familiar tune and thought the past would be pleasant if he performed it brightly enough.

He deserved to decide what his own songs meant.

"What do you want to play tonight?" I asked.

He thought about it.

"Something new."

"Then let's do that."

He smiled faintly.

"You don't even know what the new song sounds like."

"That's the exciting part."

By evening the pier was full of people carrying lanterns. Mara offered bread and warm apple cider. Iroh stood near the entrance with a pot of tea. Danse was checking the temporary lighting circuit without making anyone feel as though they had entered a military installation.

The volunteer coordinator found Greg while he was checking the set list. She had heard the stranger's request and wanted to make sure the printed program didn't list the song he'd declined.

"It won't," she said. "But a few guests still remember the old version of the show."

"Then they'll get a different one," Greg answered.

She nodded, crossed out the old title, and wrote the new song's name in pencil. There was room to change it again if Greg wanted; the program wasn't a contract to reopen a piece of grief for public consumption.

I sat beside him on the safe edge of the stage.

"Are you worried they'll be disappointed?" I asked.

"A little. Rose was important to my music. I don't hate those songs. I just don't want to play that one tonight."

"You're allowed to choose."

He looked relieved. "I know. I keep forgetting that not every request needs a good enough explanation."

We walked the cables with the technician before the audience arrived, checking that nobody would have to step over them to reach the seating. Iroh offered to help with tea and asked where the cups should go. Maui carried one bench when the crew asked and didn't attempt to move the entire stage.

"That's progress," Greg whispered.

"Don't tell him. He'll want applause."

Greg laughed. Then he leaned closer.

"Could I ask for a kiss after the show, if you're still in the mood?"

"You can ask afterward. I don't want to promise one like an encore."

He thought about it, then smiled. "Fair."

When the stage lights came on, he stood with his guitar and introduced the new song as his own choice. The audience listened. I felt proud of him, not because he'd proved that love conquered grief, but because he'd made room for a different kind of music without denying the old songs existed.

Greg took the stage after the first group of walkers had crossed the square.

The crowd quieted.

He looked down at the guitar.

Then at me.

"This one is new," he said. "It's about finding a place to sit after you've spent your whole life pretending you're fine standing up."

A few people laughed.

He played.

The melody was simple, almost shy. It had a little space between the phrases, enough that I could hear the wind in the gaps. The words didn't promise that grief would disappear. They talked about chairs, late trains, and people who kept a light on without demanding to know why someone had been gone.

It was funny and tender and entirely his.

When he finished, the applause came slowly, then grew.

The stranger in the neat jacket was in the crowd. He did not approach the stage again.

Afterward Greg climbed down and sat beside me.

"How was it?" he asked.

"Good."

"Just good?"

"Very good. I was trying not to sound like an unhelpful fan."

He laughed.

I reached for his hand. He took it and squeezed once.

"I thought you'd be angry," he said.

"I was."

"At him?"

"Yes. But I didn't want to make the evening about my anger."

He looked at me, surprised.

"That means a lot."

I leaned against his shoulder.

The lantern walk began after the concert. People moved in small groups through the square, each light bobbing in the dark. A woman carried a lantern with a painted blue wave. A child held a tiny one made of folded paper. Neri walked with no lantern at all, helping people find the accessible path.

Greg and I carried one between us.

"What does ours mean?" he asked.

I considered it.

"That we don't have to explain everything."

He smiled.

"Good answer."

We walked until the procession reached Tideglass Cove, where the sea reflected the little lights like scattered stars.

Greg set the lantern on the railing and turned toward me.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Please."

The kiss was warm and a little awkward because the guitar case kept bumping my knee. He laughed against my cheek, then kissed me again with more care.

I wanted to stay there. I wanted him to have a night where nobody needed a performance from him.

When we went back through the Starwake Door, he asked if I wanted to stay in Beach City.

"Yes," I said.

He opened the van and put the guitar away.

The rest of the night belonged to us, not to an audience.

In the morning, he found the program the stranger had left near the stage. He folded it once and set it in the recycling basket.

Then he picked up his guitar and began writing another song.

Not because anybody had asked.

Because he wanted to.
